argument.reply:
In Kantian deontology, duties are ranked by strictness. Promise-keeping is a perfect duty: its violation cannot be coherently universalised because a world in which promises are routinely broken would destroy the institution of promising itself. Rescuing strangers is an imperfect duty of beneficence: we must sometimes help, but the maxim "always save the person with the highest chance of survival" can be willed universally without contradiction; its non-performance in a given instance does not invalidate the practice of beneficence. Hence, when a perfect and an imperfect duty conflict, the perfect duty has lexical priority.

argument.target: Why should your preferred duty take priority over the competing rescue or fidelity claim?
argument.reply: Within Kantian deontology the promise to Cara generates a perfect duty of fidelity. A perfect duty forbids the contradictory opposite (making a promise one intends to break); universalising that maxim would destroy the institution of promising. The rescue of Ben is an imperfect duty of beneficence because Ada has no special tie to Ben beyond general concern for others. Imperfect duties admit latitude; they obligate adopting some maxims of aid, not every possible specific aid. When two duties conflict, Kant holds that perfect duties set strict constraints on maxims that imperfect duties cannot override. Therefore, breaking the promise is categorically impermissible, whereas failing this particular rescue is a permissible (though regrettable) omission consistent with still adopting other beneficent maxims.
argument.framework_commitment: Kant: perfect duties (e.g., fidelity) have priority over imperfect duties (e.g., beneficence).
argument.reasoning_bridge: Classify promise-keeping as perfect duty; classify rescuing stranger as imperfect beneficence; apply Kantian hierarchy to resolve conflict.
argument.remaining_uncertainty: Whether life-threatening stakes can elevate beneficence here to a perfect positive duty of rescue; whether the promise was valid given resource scarcity.
argument.reversal_condition: If Ben’s rescue constituted a perfect positive duty (e.g., special obligation or universally necessary aid), or if the promise was invalid, then duty priority could reverse.

argument.reply: The imperfect duty of beneficence already binds Ada to try to save a life when she can. That duty does not change when the stated probabilities move; what shifts is how well each available act can realize that same duty. As long as both patients are strangers and neither has a special claim, the duty gives Ada latitude but also requires that the adopted maxim be capable of being a universal law. A maxim such as “When I must choose which of two strangers to treat, I will give the treatment where it has the higher chance of success” can be willed universally because it seeks the same end of aiding others while using available resources rationally. If the probabilities reversed, the same duty would direct the medicine to the now-better-off patient. Thus the comparative numbers do not create a new duty but guide the practical specification of the existing one.
